speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (on behalf of the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: IDA is part of the World Bank Group.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (on behalf of the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: It provides concessional loans to its least developed member countries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (on behalf of the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Currently, section 4 of the IDA Act allows the Government to pay for subscriptions to IDA, up to a cumulative "total subscription" cap of US$1 million.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (on behalf of the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: It also allows the Government to seek Parliament's approval to increase the cap, as the Government did in 2016 and 2019.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (on behalf of the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Parliament will, therefore, remain as the approving authority over any such expenditure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (on behalf of the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Under the previous voting rights framework, only a small part of the contributions made by a country would result in "subscription votes".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (on behalf of the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: However, under the new voting rights framework, all new contributions to IDA replenishments will equate to subscriptions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (on behalf of the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: This change in method affects all IDA members.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (on behalf of the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: With this change by IDA, we can no longer meaningfully compare past and future votes, as the unit of measurement is no longer the same.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (on behalf of the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: We are proposing to amend the Act to reflect these changes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (on behalf of the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Singapore will continue to contribute our fair share to IDA as a responsible global stakeholder, while ensuring financial prudence and spending within our means.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, a new subsection is added to make provision for the maximum amount of any additional subscription to be specified and to be authorised by a separate resolution of Parliament.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: As has been pointed out in this House by Second Minister for Finance, Ms Indranee Rajah, in November 2019, since Singapore joined the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, a major institution of the World Bank Group that makes loans to developing countries, in 1966, it has received 12 loans to support various infrastructure projects.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: This means that for a decade after Singapore became fully independent, our country benefited from external loans that supported our journey on the path of economic development.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Economists have grappled with the question of what it takes to make a poor country become rich.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: They do not have a fully satisfactory answer.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: While alleviating the problem of poverty in developing countries is such an important task, the approach to achieving it is still not so well understood.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: While we know the proximate causes of economic growth in the sense that a higher standard of living can be explained by a higher level of applied technology and a higher level of human capital and physical capital per worker, less is known about the fundamental causes of economic growth.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: What are the underlying reasons why some countries are unable or unwilling to invest in capital and technology?

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Despite our limited knowledge, we do have many examples of countries that have experienced growth take-offs that raise the quality of life of their citizens.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Our own experience – the Singapore experience – suggests that when political and economic institutions are set up that support an integration with the global economy to facilitate the transfer of technology, we achieve a growth take-off.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Along the growth path, the extension of external loans to finance infrastructural projects enables the country to overcome capital market constraints, especially when the investment is lumpy.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's subscription to IDA as a donor country allows us to contribute to a global fund that can potentially enable other countries to get onto a path of economic development, just as Singapore did.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: There is a wide gap in the standard of living between poor and rich countries.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Some economists have argued that geography plays a big part in explaining why some countries remain poor despite the availability of frontier technology that can be tapped for growth.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Unfavourable soil conditions may make it hard to develop agriculture, for example, and many countries tend to have to develop their agriculture first before manufacturing can become an increasing share of the GDP.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: For such countries, a lack of navigable rivers and poor access to sea transport may make it difficult for them to effectively make use of their factors of production.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Communities might also be disadvantaged economically when climatic conditions lead to widespread diseases, such as malaria and dengue fever, that affect a large proportion of the labour force.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: For them, therefore, concessional loans can be made available, through IDA, to finance large-scale investments in transport infrastructure and disease eradication to partially overcome these geographical disadvantages.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: I think that Singapore can make a meaningful contribution to this global effort.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Today, we have the world's largest container transhipment hub-port.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There is a Chinese saying 饮水思源 – when we drink water, we must remember where it came from.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And when we are able to do so, we shall pay it forward to help others.
